extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent examiners and patent applicants (prosecutors and agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for Canadian patent examiners (and applicants) on examination practice including purposive claim construction, prior art searching, suspension rules, and examiner reporting requirements. Covers steps for construing claims, identifying POSITA and common general knowledge, determining essential elements, search scope, and when to communicate defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter should identify multiple matters in single submission
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant chooses to include multiple matters in a single submission pertaining to an application or patent, the applicant should clearly indicate these requests on the first page of the cover letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of such matters include submission of prior art, appointment and revocation of agent, request for examination, request for advanced examination, maintenance fee. Where an amendment submission also includes a PPH request form, this should also be mentioned in the cover letter. Incoming correspondence is manually sorted and may not be processed in the order dispatched, so clear identification helps proper treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension of examination — grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Under subsection 86(17) of the Patent Rules, the examination of patent applications is suspended in specified situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspension occurs during the late fee period if the maintenance fee is unpaid (suspension begins on the maintenance fee due date and ends when both maintenance and late fees are paid), and during any period of deemed abandonment (examination resumes when the application is reinstated). While suspended, applicants will not typically receive reports or notices from the examiner; however, notices sent or received during suspension are still valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of examination
rubrics_metrics.description: At each stage, perform a thorough analysis of the patent application to determine whether it complies with the requirements of the Patent Act and Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of this analysis the examiner performs a purposive construction of the claims and considers a search of the prior art. If compliant, the examiner will approve the application for allowance (notice of allowance); if not, defects may be communicated via an examiner's report, examiner-initiated interview, or a conditional notice of allowance. An application may be examined before being laid open, but allowance or conditional notice will not be issued until laid open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of abstract, description and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract, description and drawings are subject to detailed examination as part of determining compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed discussions on each are found in chapters 13 (abstract), 14 (description) and 15 (drawings) of the MOPOP (referenced for specifics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposive construction required for claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner’s identification of the actual invention must be grounded in a purposive construction of the patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposive construction must take into account the role of the patent examiner and the purpose and context of examination. It is performed to determine what the person skilled in the art would have understood the applicant to have intended as the scope of protection as of the date of publication of the application. Once a claim has been purposively construed, that construction is used to determine compliance with the Patent Act and Patent Rules. If there is no disagreement as to construction, the examiner may choose not to provide detailed purposive construction analysis in a report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for non-English/French text matter in construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Text matter that is not in English or French in certain sequence listings or PCT national application parts should not be taken into account for interpreting scope of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: text matter not in English or French in the sequence listing of a regular Canadian application, or in the specification or drawings of a PCT national application, should not be used to interpret scope unless that text matter is in free text of a sequence listing, in a non-language dependent field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steps of purposive construction
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining a claim, an examiner must read the claim in an informed and purposive way, performing specific preliminary steps before construing the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to construing a claim an examiner will: identify the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) and identify the relevant common general knowledge (CGK) of that person at the time of publication. Once context is determined the examiner will identify the problem addressed and its solution as contemplated by the inventor, and determine the meaning of claim terms and identify elements essential to solve the identified problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a fair, balanced and informed approach to construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction requires a fair, balanced and informed approach considering the specification as a whole and the common general knowledge of the POSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms of a claim receive technical meanings in light of CGK. The specification provides the context and must be read through the eyes of the POSITA. Foundation of knowledge comes from applicant submissions and the examiner’s technical expertise. A properly informed purposive construction considers the specification as a whole against the background CGK at the relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the person skilled in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before construing claims, the examiner must identify the person skilled in the art: a fictitious construct representing an average competent worker in the relevant field(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: POSITA may be an individual or a team; is logical but unimaginative (not a creative expert); in highly technical fields may be presumed to have expert-level knowledge; need not be a manufacturer or designer but must understand the problem and means to address it; reasonably diligent, may be multilingual; may have knowledge from outside the field but not presumed. Exact educational background or experience is typically unnecessary. If POSITA is relevant to resolving an issue, the examiner will determine who this person is by reference to relevant fields and consider applicant comments; characterisation should be careful but generalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the common general knowledge (CGK)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the POSITA, the examiner must identify the relevant common general knowledge of that person at the relevant date (publication date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CGK means knowledge generally known by persons skilled in the relevant art at the relevant time. It distinguishes widely recognised information (common themes from the 'forest of art') from merely publicly available disclosures. CGK can be established by reference works (textbooks, review articles, handbooks) or by demonstrating commonality across a number of disclosures; subsequent publications may confirm CGK. Examiners may rely on information they believe to have been CGK unless the applicant disputes it. Statements in the application's description that certain information is commonly known may be relied upon without verification, and the applicant is bound to such comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the problem and solution
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of the problem addressed by the inventor and the solution provided informs purposive construction: an invention is an inventive solution to a practical problem and must be disclosed to provide an operable solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The problem need not be explicitly stated; paragraph 56(1)(d) requires description to permit the technical problem and its solution to be understood even if not expressly stated. Identification is guided by the examiner’s understanding of CGK and teachings of the description. Focus in description on particular details can indicate the problem; the examiner should consider the background, objects, specific problems, needs, limitations or disadvantages stated by the inventor. Claim construction cannot be determined solely literally — it must consider the application as a whole to avoid 'pitfalls of language'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine essential elements that solve the identified problem
rubrics_metrics.description: One must identify which claim elements are essential to provide the solution to the problem; this is central to purposive construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essential elements cannot be identified without first identifying the problem and solution. Some elements that materially affect an embodiment may nonetheless be non-essential if the skilled addressee would have appreciated they could be substituted or omitted. An element is essential if required to provide the solution regardless of whether it is known. Essentiality is not determined merely by whether an element distinguishes over prior art or is part of CGK. If a claim omits an essential element, it may be defective for over-breadth (lack of support) and/or lack of utility. Superfluous (non-essential) elements are not a defect per se but could render a claim ambiguous. If a claim includes solutions to more than one problem, examination should focus on one solution, guided by the description's emphasis. Aggregation (elements not interacting) versus combination should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination after claim construction — reporting and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: After purposive construction, examine whether essential elements clearly define subject-matter that complies with statutory requirements and provide reasons where relevant to perceived defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners need not explain conclusions in a report unless there is disagreement; parts of analysis not in issue need not be detailed. Where conclusions about specific elements are relevant to an identified defect, the examiner should provide reasons (emphasize problem and solution and elements essential to that solution). Specific statutory requirements addressed in later chapters: clarity and form (Chapter 16), subject matter (17), utility (19), novelty/obviousness/double patenting (18).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrative examples to apply purposive construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the purposive construction guidance through concrete examples to determine POSITA, CGK, problem, solution, essential elements, and whether claims are statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (skillet and spoon with specific identifier; outdoor playpen with sensors; board game scenarios) illustrate how to identify the problem and solution, distinguish essential elements, and determine statutory subject-matter (e.g., purely aesthetic 'specific identifier' leading to non-statutory claim). Examiners should follow the analytical steps shown in examples when assessing similar fact patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art search scope and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability must be assessed in view of the prior art, broadly including all information made available to the public prior to the claim date, with limited exceptions for applicant disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice prior art relied on during examination generally comprises published patent documents, journal articles, textbooks, manuals and the like. An application may result from a national filing or PCT national phase entry; scope of a Canadian examiner's search at national phase is influenced by earlier searches. Examiners are not required to search claimed matter having defects relating to unity of invention, divisional requirements, or new matter. Where a comprehensive international search exists, a Canadian examiner will nevertheless perform at least a Canadian patent document search for double-patenting or anticipation concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign search results and further searching
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may consider available foreign search results to avoid duplicative work, but should indicate when they rely on foreign-identified documents and may undertake further searches as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on foreign search results in a report the examiner should indicate which documents were identified in the foreign search. Further searches need not be restricted to Canadian documents and can use any databases available to the examiner. Searches are generally limited by combinations of dates, keywords, and IPC codes. While desirable to identify all relevant prior art in the first report, documents may be missed and additional relevant art may be identified later; examiners must cite relevant prior art identified during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to cite relevant prior art discovered during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where relevant prior art is identified during prosecution, the examiner is incumbent to cite it against the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the volume of prior art, documents may be missed at early stages; however, any relevant prior art found later must be cited in the record and relied upon as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of examiner's reports (requisitions under subsection 86(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner’s report is an official means of communicating with an applicant that identifies defects in the application and contains a requisition under subsection 86(2) or 86(5) of the Patent Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under subsection 86(2), where an examiner has reasonable grounds to believe an application does not comply with the Patent Act and Patent Rules, the applicant must be informed of the defects and requisitioned to amend the application to comply or to provide arguments as to why the application does comply. Reports may take the form of a Final Action (see Chapter 26).
